# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

questions.question: Key the limit on x-customer-id, client IP, or both?

brief.where: `src/server.ts:7-8` requires `x-customer-id` on every request and it is the only identity in the system — unverified, client-supplied, and already trusted for writes (`createOrder(customerId, …)`). Three instances sit behind a round-robin LB, so per-IP keying needs `X-Forwarded-For` (spoofable unless the LB overwrites it) or Bun's `server.requestIP()` (returns the LB's address unless proxy protocol is on). 20 enterprise customers burst legitimately, and some likely share egress IPs.
brief.what: The key determines what a 'customer' means to the limiter, and every later number, override and error message hangs off it. The header is unauthenticated, so customer-id-only is advisory for anyone who rotates the header; IP-only collides enterprises behind one NAT and is blind behind an LB.
brief.how: Pick the recommended pair and the limit is expressed per customer with a coarse anti-rotation ceiling; other answers change the required LB/header plumbing and who gets punished when one script misbehaves.

evidence.note: header is read and trusted with no verification
customerId flows straight into the write

options.label: Yes — customer id primary + coarse per-IP ceiling
options.tradeoff: Limits are meaningful per customer; the IP ceiling catches header rotation, but needs XFF handling at the LB and a ceiling far above enterprise burst so shared NAT never trips it.
options.description: Per-customer token bucket as the real limit; a second, much looser IP-level budget purely as a safety net.
options.holds_when: The LB can be made to overwrite X-Forwarded-For (or we accept requestIP once it returns the client).

options.label: Customer id only
options.tradeoff: Simplest and zero LB work; a hostile script rotating x-customer-id is unlimited, so this is fairness, not protection.
options.description: One budget per distinct header value.

options.label: IP only
options.tradeoff: Not spoofable at L3 if XFF is trustworthy, but enterprise NATs collapse into one bucket and the customer dimension disappears from the data.
options.description: Budget per source address.

options.label: Customer id now, verify the header before trusting it
options.tradeoff: The only option that makes the limiter non-advisory; adds an auth/key-rotation project (shared secret, mTLS or signed token) that cannot ship this week.
options.description: Introduce identity verification first, then key everything on the verified id.

questions.question: Does the limit cover only POST /orders, or every route per customer?

brief.where: Only two routes exist: `POST /orders` (Postgres insert, the expensive one) and `GET /orders` (Postgres select per the plan's description). The incident was 40,000 POSTs in ten minutes.
brief.what: A limiter on POST alone leaves a script free to hammer GET and still slow everyone else; a shared budget makes a busy read customer unable to write. This also fixes what the limit's unit is (writes vs requests), which the enterprise numbers depend on.
brief.how: POST-only keeps the unit 'orders created', which enterprise customers can reason about and which matches the incident; adding GET forces a second unit and doubles the numbers to agree.

options.label: Yes — POST /orders only
options.tradeoff: Matches the incident and keeps one legible unit; leaves a read-storm hole that nobody has hit yet.
options.description: One per-customer budget expressed in order creations.

options.label: POST + GET under one shared per-customer budget
options.tradeoff: Closes the read hole; couples reads and writes so a customer polling GET can exhaust its write budget.
options.description: One request budget over both routes.

options.label: POST + GET with separate budgets
options.tradeoff: Correct semantics and closes the hole; requires two sets of numbers per customer tier and more config surface.
options.description: Write budget and read budget per customer.

questions.question: Fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket?

brief.where: The plan's workload is 20 customers that legitimately burst against a baseline, and one script doing 40k in ten minutes (~67/s sustained). No metrics exist in the repo to say what a legitimate peak looks like.
brief.what: The algorithm decides what 'legitimate burst' means and how precisely a client can be told when to retry. Fixed window allows 2x the limit across a boundary (bad for the exact case we are fixing); sliding-window-log stores one entry per request (40k keys per abuser); token bucket stores two numbers and lets burst capacity be tuned independently of sustained rate — which is exactly the enterprise-burst shape.
brief.how: Token bucket lets the burst capacity be a policy knob separate from the refill rate, and yields an exact retry delay for Retry-After; fixed window makes the enterprise numbers need a safety factor for the boundary exploit.

evidence.note: bursty-but-legitimate traffic plus one sustained abuser

options.label: Yes — token bucket (GCRA)
options.tradeoff: Two-integer state per key, exact retry delay, tunable burst; slightly more code than a counter and needs a small Lua/atomic script in Redis.
options.description: Capacity = burst allowance, refill = sustained rate; a rejected request does not consume a token.

options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Trivial to implement; admits up to 2x the limit at window edges and punishes enterprises that legitimately burst at minute boundaries.
options.description: Counter per minute bucket.

options.label: Sliding window
options.tradeoff: Smoothest behaviour, but the log variant is memory-heavy per abuser and the counter variant is extra machinery for a first ship.
options.description: Log or weighted-two-bucket moving window.

questions.question: Where do counters live: shared Redis, per-instance memory, or Postgres?

brief.where: Three instances receive round-robin requests, so per-instance memory means each instance sees ~1/3 of a customer's traffic: an in-memory limit of N produces ~3N globally and inconsistent decisions per request. Redis 7 is available but owned by another service (sessions) and 'we may use it'. Postgres is already a dependency but is the resource being protected. The repo has no package.json; Bun ships a Redis client, so no third-party dependency is strictly required (verify against the deployed Bun version).
brief.what: This is the coupling decision: sharing another team's Redis buys atomic global counts at the cost of blast radius and an eviction/ACL risk; memory buys independence at the cost of the limit meaning nothing; Postgres adds write amplification to the exact bottleneck being defended.
brief.how: Once the store is chosen, the failure mode question (fail-open vs closed), the counter-key layout and whether limits can be changed without a deploy all follow from it.

evidence.note: Postgres is the only shared dependency in the code today

options.label: Yes — existing Redis cluster, dedicated keyspace + ACL
options.tradeoff: Atomic global counts for free; depends on the owning team granting a separate logical DB/ACL and guaranteeing no eviction of our keys, and puts a new failure mode in the request path.
options.description: Reuse the session cluster with a `rl:` prefix, separate credentials, and explicit no-eviction handling.
options.holds_when: The owning team agrees to a dedicated logical DB and the cluster's maxmemory policy cannot evict our keys.

options.label: Dedicated new Redis instance
options.tradeoff: No blast radius and no negotiation; one more thing to run, secure and page someone for, likely past this week's ship date.
options.description: Own Redis for rate limits only.

options.label: Per-instance in-memory
options.tradeoff: Zero infrastructure; the limit must be divided by 3 and is still wrong under uneven balancing or a rolling deploy that resets counters.
options.description: Local token buckets, limit per instance = global/3.

options.label: Postgres counter table
options.tradeoff: Reuses an existing dependency with no new service; adds a write (and row contention) to the database we are trying to protect.
options.description: Atomic increment/upsert per customer in Postgres.

questions.question: What does a throttled client see?

brief.where: Existing errors are plain text with no code (`401 "missing x-customer-id"`, `404 "not found"` in `src/server.ts:8,17`); successes are JSON. 20 enterprise scripted integrations will parse whatever we return.
brief.what: This is a client-visible contract they must code against, so it must be decided before any shadow rollout is announced. It also fixes whether the retry hint is machine-readable (Retry-After, exact second under a token bucket) and whether throttling is distinguishable from a real 4xx bug in their logs.
brief.how: A JSON envelope with a stable code lets integrations branch on throttling without string matching; Retry-After lets them back off correctly instead of retry-storming the limiter.

evidence.note: current error shape is plain text

options.label: Yes — 429 + Retry-After + JSON body with a code
options.tradeoff: Unambiguous and machine-actionable; a new error shape that differs from the existing plain-text 401/404, so it needs a doc/announcement to the 20 integrations.
options.description: `429`, `Retry-After: <seconds>`, `{"error":{"code":"rate_limited","retry_after_seconds":N}}`.

options.label: 429 + plain text
options.tradeoff: Consistent with today's errors and zero client doc work; clients must string-match or retry blindly.
options.description: `429 "rate limited"`.

options.label: 429 + JSON + RateLimit-* headers
options.tradeoff: Gives clients proactive budget visibility; more surface to get right and to keep consistent under multiple instances.
options.description: Standard RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset headers on every response.
